Pain is plausible after surgery, but restlessness with tachycardia and hypotension is a perfusion warning. Treating pain first misreads an unexpected finding as an expected one.
A correct routine postoperative measure, but it does not address the unstable circulation and could tire a client in early shock.
strategy: Early recognition: trend and ABC
keyFacts: Rising pulse with falling blood pressure, cool clammy skin and restlessness after surgery suggests hemorrhage or shock until proven otherwise.
A dry dressing does not exclude internal bleeding.

vignette: In the post-anesthesia care unit, a client who had general anesthesia 20 minutes ago is difficult to rouse and has noisy, snoring respirations. Oxygen saturation is falling slowly. The intravenous site at the left forearm looks swollen, and the blood pressure is 150/88 mm Hg.
stem: Which action should the nurse perform first?
options: Stop the infusion and restart the intravenous line in the other arm.
Apply supplemental oxygen at the prescribed flow through a mask.
Open the airway with a jaw-thrust or head-tilt chin-lift maneuver.
Repeat the blood pressure on the opposite arm to confirm the reading.
rationale: 1) List the problems: snoring breathing and falling saturation, infiltrated IV, mildly raised blood pressure. 2) Apply ABC: airway before breathing before circulation. 3) Snoring in a sedated client points to soft-tissue obstruction, an airway problem that is present now. 4) Oxygen (breathing) is tempting, but it works best once the airway is open. 5) The IV and blood pressure are circulation items and not immediately life-threatening. 6) Choose the maneuver that opens the airway.
optionRationales: Infiltration needs attention, but it is a circulation or comfort concern of lower priority than a compromised airway.
Breathing support is important and likely needed, but oxygen delivered past an obstructed airway is less effective; the airway is opened before breathing is supported.
Snoring respirations in a poorly responsive client usually mean the tongue is partially blocking the airway. Airway comes first in ABC and the maneuver takes seconds.
A mildly high pressure after surgery is not the immediate threat and rechecking it does not address the declining oxygen saturation.
strategy: ABC: airway first
keyFacts: Snoring respirations in a sedated or unconscious client suggest partial airway obstruction.
Open the airway before giving oxygen.

vignette: A nurse on a medical unit receives report on four clients. One has pneumonia and is newly confused with respirations 28/min and oxygen saturation 86% (it was 94% this morning). One has chronic lung disease on low-flow oxygen with mild breathlessness at baseline and saturation 91%. One is on day 1 after appendectomy with pain 4/10 and wants to walk. One has cellulitis and the next antibiotic dose is due in 30 minutes.
stem: Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: The client with pneumonia who is newly confused with a saturation of 86%
The client with chronic lung disease on low-flow oxygen with saturation 91%
The client on day 1 after appendectomy with pain rated 4/10 who wants to walk
The client with cellulitis whose next antibiotic dose is due in 30 minutes
rationale: 1) Read the stem: it asks who to see first, so rank the clients. 2) Label each by stability: only the pneumonia client has a new and worsening change. 3) Fall in saturation from 94% to 86% plus confusion and fast respirations signals hypoxemia (oxygenation, the highest Maslow need). 4) The client with chronic lung disease looks serious but the numbers are that client's baseline. 5) The postoperative and cellulitis clients are stable with routine needs. 6) Choose the new, unstable oxygenation problem.
optionRationales: New confusion with a falling saturation and fast breathing indicates worsening hypoxemia. New and unstable outranks stable or expected findings.
Tempting because of the lung disease, but the findings are chronic and match the client's usual status, so this client is stable.
Pain is a physiological need, but it is moderate and expected after surgery, and the client is mobile and stable.
A time-sensitive medication, but the client is stable and the dose is not yet due.
strategy: Triage: unstable and new before stable
keyFacts: New confusion in a client with pneumonia can be an early sign of hypoxemia.
Compare findings to the client's baseline before ranking.

vignette: A 72-year-old client is on the first night after major abdominal surgery and uses a patient-controlled opioid pump. At 0300 the nurse finds the client difficult to arouse, with slow shallow respirations at 8 per minute. The nurse stops the pump. The arterial blood gas result shows a pH below the normal range, a carbon dioxide level above the normal range, and a bicarbonate level within normal limits. The provider has been paged but has not yet called back.
stem: The nurse is at the bedside and the pump is stopped. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Place an oxygen mask on the client and reassess the oxygen saturation in ten minutes
Ask the provider for an order for an opioid reversal agent and wait to hear back before acting
Draw a repeat arterial blood sample to confirm the carbon dioxide trend before intervening
Rouse the client firmly by voice and touch and reposition the airway to support breathing
rationale: 1) Read the gas: low pH with high carbon dioxide and normal bicarbonate means acute respiratory acidosis, so the body has not had time to compensate. 2) Link it to the history: sedating drug, hard to arouse, rate of 8 per minute, so the client is hypoventilating. 3) Maslow and ABC: breathing is the threat and the client is unstable, so the nurse acts at the bedside now. 4) The drug source is already stopped, so the next step is to support ventilation by rousing the client and opening the airway. 5) Oxygen alone, a repeat sample, and waiting for an order each delay direct support of breathing. 6) A reversal agent may be needed, but it requires an order and does not replace airway support while waiting.
optionRationales: Oxygen is right for low oxygen, but this problem is retained carbon dioxide from slow breathing. A mask with a ten-minute wait leaves the client unsupported and hides worsening drowsiness.
A reversal agent may be part of the plan, but it needs a provider order and takes time. The nurse does not stand by while the client is under-breathing; direct support of breathing comes first.
The result is already clear and a second sample would be the right follow-up later. Collecting it before intervening treats a number while the client is deteriorating.
Rousing the client and repositioning the airway directly supports breathing at the bedside, which is the first priority for an unstable client with respiratory acidosis from opioid sedation.
strategy: ABC: breathing before results and orders
keyFacts: High carbon dioxide with low pH and normal bicarbonate indicates acute respiratory acidosis, often from hypoventilation.
Opioid sedation is a leading cause of postoperative hypoventilation; breathing support comes before further testing or waiting for orders.

vignette: A 49-year-old client is admitted with a three-week cough, night sweats, weight loss and blood-streaked sputum. The provider suspects active pulmonary tuberculosis. The nurse is arranging the client's room and personal protective equipment.
stem: Which precaution is most appropriate?
options: Place the client in a negative-pressure room and wear a fitted respirator when entering.
Place the client in a private room and wear a standard surgical mask when entering the room.
Use a private room, wear a gown and gloves for contact with the client, and keep the door open.
Use standard precautions in a shared room until the sputum culture result confirms the diagnosis.
rationale: 1) Identify the suspected organism and its route of spread: tuberculosis is airborne. 2) Recall which precaution type matches: airborne uses negative pressure and a respirator. 3) Eliminate droplet (surgical mask) and contact (gown and gloves) as wrong routes. 4) Eliminate standard-only: precautions start on suspicion, not confirmation. 5) Choose negative-pressure room plus fitted respirator.
optionRationales: Tuberculosis spreads by small airborne particles, so airborne precautions with a negative-pressure room and a fitted respirator are used. The client wears a surgical mask during transport.
Matches droplet precautions, tempting because the illness is respiratory, but a surgical mask does not filter airborne particles.
Describes contact precautions, which fit skin or wound organisms, and an open door would allow airborne particles to leave.
Waiting for confirmation exposes staff and other clients; precautions begin when the disease is suspected.
strategy: Infection: match route to precaution
keyFacts: Airborne precautions: negative-pressure room and fitted respirator for tuberculosis, measles and chickenpox.
Start isolation on suspicion, before confirmation.

vignette: A 77-year-old client who has been taking a broad-spectrum antibiotic for several days develops frequent watery stools. The provider suspects infection with Clostridioides difficile. The nurse prepares to provide care in the client's private room.
stem: Which action is most appropriate to prevent spread?
options: Wear a surgical mask and clean hands with an alcohol-based rub before leaving the room.
Wear gloves for care and clean hands with an alcohol-based rub after removing them.
Wear a gown and gloves, and wash with soap and water after removing them.
Move the client to a negative-pressure room and wear a fitted respirator for care.
rationale: 1) Identify the route: this organism spreads by contact with feces and contaminated surfaces. 2) Match to contact precautions with gown and gloves. 3) Recall the special rule: spores survive alcohol, so soap and water are used. 4) Eliminate options with masks or respirators because the route is not respiratory. 5) Eliminate the option that relies on alcohol rub. 6) Choose gown, gloves and soap-and-water handwashing.
optionRationales: A mask is the droplet measure, and alcohol rub is a common habit that is not dependable against spores.
Gloves are needed, but a gown is also required when clothing may touch the client or surfaces, and alcohol rub is less effective here.
This organism forms spores that alcohol-based rubs do not reliably kill, so contact precautions with soap-and-water handwashing are used.
Airborne precautions are not needed for a gut organism spread by the fecal-oral route.
strategy: Infection: match route to precaution
keyFacts: Soap and water handwashing is preferred when caring for clients with suspected spore-forming diarrheal infection.
Contact precautions use a gown and gloves.

vignette: A nurse is teaching a 68-year-old client with chronic lung disease who will start home oxygen from a concentrator. A relative who smokes visits often. The nurse asks the client to describe how oxygen will be used safely at home.
stem: Which statement by the client shows a need for further teaching?
options: "I will ask visitors who smoke to stay outside and I will post a no-smoking sign."
"I will keep the concentrator away from the stove and other heat sources."
"I will keep a backup supply and the supplier's phone number ready."
"If I feel more short of breath, I will turn up the flow to a higher setting."
rationale: 1) Notice the stem asks which statement shows a NEED for teaching, so look for the unsafe statement. 2) Evaluate each as safe or unsafe: smoking and heat avoidance are correct; a backup supply is correct. 3) Self-adjusting the flow is the one that conflicts with safe practice. 4) Oxygen is a medication and is changed only on the provider's order; worsening breathlessness should be reported. 5) Choose the incorrect statement.
optionRationales: Shows understanding; oxygen supports combustion, so smoking and open flames are kept away.
Appropriate fire-safety practice, so no further teaching is needed.
A sensible plan in case of equipment or power problems, so it reflects understanding.
Flow is changed only as prescribed. Raising oxygen alone can be harmful in some chronic lung conditions and hides worsening disease that needs to be reported.
strategy: Teaching: teach-back accuracy
keyFacts: Oxygen supports combustion: no smoking, open flames or heat sources nearby.
Do not change the oxygen flow rate without an order.

vignette: A nurse is caring for a 66-year-old client with heart failure who takes a loop diuretic daily and has had several episodes of vomiting over two days. During morning assessment the nurse notes four findings: increased urine output since the last shift, a weight lower than yesterday, mild thirst with dry lips, and new generalized muscle weakness with an irregular pulse.
stem: Which finding is most concerning and requires follow-up?
options: Increased urine output compared with the last shift
New muscle weakness along with an irregular pulse
A lower weight on the scale than yesterday morning
Mild thirst with dry lips after repeated vomiting
rationale: 1) Identify the context: a diuretic plus vomiting leads to fluid and electrolyte loss. 2) Sort the findings into expected effects of treatment and unexpected or dangerous ones. 3) Increased urine output and falling weight are the intended effects. 4) Mild thirst is minor and easily corrected. 5) Weakness with an irregular pulse suggests a low potassium level affecting muscle and heart, a circulation threat. 6) Choose the unexpected finding with the highest risk.
optionRationales: Expected with a loop diuretic, so it is not a warning sign by itself.
Potassium loss from the diuretic and vomiting can cause weakness and heart rhythm changes. An irregular pulse is a dangerous, unexpected finding.
Expected when fluid is being removed in heart failure; the nurse would continue to monitor.
Plausible after vomiting and diuresis and worth addressing, but it is less threatening than a possible rhythm disturbance.
strategy: Expected vs unexpected finding
keyFacts: Low potassium can cause muscle weakness and cardiac rhythm changes.
Loop diuretics and vomiting both cause potassium loss.

topic: Neutropenic fever versus other chemotherapy effects
vignette: A 61-year-old client is on day 8 after a cycle of chemotherapy, and this morning's laboratory report shows a very low neutrophil count. The client is sitting in a chair and says nothing hurts. During the shift the nurse notes four findings in the chart and at the bedside, and must decide which one to act on first.
stem: Which finding should the nurse act on first?
options: Mouth sores that make swallowing tablets painful this morning
Fatigue so marked that help is needed to reach the bathroom
Temperature of 38.3 C in a client who says they feel fine
Vomiting twice this shift with half the meal tray eaten
rationale: 1) All four findings can occur after chemotherapy, so first sort expected effects from dangerous ones. 2) Use the lab data: very low neutrophils means the usual defenses against infection are weak. 3) In this state fever may be the earliest and sometimes the only sign of infection, so the client's comfort does not lower the priority. 4) Mouth sores, marked fatigue with a fall risk, and vomiting all need nursing care, but none is as quickly life-threatening. 5) Choose the fever and report it promptly.
optionRationales: Painful mouth sores need pain relief and a way to take medication, but they are an expected effect and not an immediate threat to life.
Fatigue with a fall risk needs help and a safety plan, which is a real concern, but the risk can be managed at once and is not rapidly fatal.
With very low neutrophils, a fever may be the only warning of serious infection that can progress quickly to sepsis, even when the client feels well. This is treated as an emergency.
Vomiting and reduced intake need antiemetic and fluid follow-up, but this is an expected effect that can be managed while the fever is reported.
strategy: Unstable or life-threatening before expected effects
keyFacts: Fever in a client with very low neutrophils is a medical emergency, even if the client feels well.
Chemotherapy lowers white cells for a period after each cycle, and the usual signs of infection may be blunted.

vignette: The nurse is assigning tasks for a surgical unit to an unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) member. The tasks are: assessing the drainage and breath sounds of a client with a chest tube placed this morning; teaching incentive spirometry to a client on day 1 after surgery; obtaining routine vital signs for a client on day 3 after an uncomplicated hernia repair; and evaluating the pain relief achieved after an intravenous opioid dose.
stem: Which task is most appropriate to delegate?
options: Taking routine vital signs for the stable client after a hernia repair
Assessing the drainage and breath sounds of the client with a new chest tube
Teaching a client on day 1 after surgery how to use the incentive spirometer
Evaluating the client's pain relief after the intravenous opioid dose
rationale: 1) Recall that delegation covers stable, routine, predictable tasks. 2) Assessment, teaching and evaluation stay with the licensed nurse. 3) Check each task against those limits: chest tube assessment is assessment of a new, less stable situation. 4) Incentive spirometry teaching is teaching; pain evaluation is evaluation. 5) Routine vital signs in a stable client is the only task that fits, with the nurse interpreting results. 6) Choose the vital signs task.
optionRationales: This is a routine, predictable task for a stable client. The nurse still interprets the results and follows up on abnormal readings.
Assessment of a recent chest tube client requires licensed judgment and cannot be delegated.
Initial teaching is a nursing responsibility; the UAP may remind a client to use the device after the nurse has taught it.
Evaluation of drug effect and the client's response is part of the nursing process and is not delegated.
strategy: Delegation: stable and routine only
keyFacts: Delegate tasks, not judgment: assessment, teaching and evaluation stay with the nurse.
A nurse remains accountable for interpreting delegated data.

topic: Priority diagnosis in chronic lung disease
vignette: A 65-year-old client with chronic lung disease is admitted with a flare of breathlessness. The client is anxious about missing a family event, has little knowledge about inhaler technique, and is at some risk for infection because of prolonged hospital stay. Respirations are 26/min with use of accessory muscles and saturation is 88% on room air.
stem: Which nursing diagnosis has the highest priority?
options: Anxiety related to missing an important family event
Deficient knowledge related to correct inhaler technique
Risk for infection related to prolonged hospital stay
Impaired gas exchange related to retained secretions
rationale: 1) List the needs and label them: oxygenation (physiological), anxiety (psychosocial), knowledge deficit (teaching), risk for infection (potential). 2) Apply Maslow: physiological before psychosocial. 3) Apply actual before potential: low saturation and accessory muscle use are present now. 4) Teaching comes after stabilization. 5) Choose the gas exchange diagnosis.
optionRationales: A real concern, but psychosocial needs rank below an unmet physiological need.
Teaching is appropriate after the client's breathing is stabilized.
A potential problem; an actual oxygenation problem outranks a risk.
Oxygenation is the most basic physiological need and the problem is actual and present, with low saturation and accessory muscle use.
strategy: Maslow: physiological first
keyFacts: Oxygenation is a basic physiological need and ranks first.
An actual problem outranks a risk (potential) problem.

topic: Responding to a client considering refusal of cancer treatment
vignette: A 54-year-old client who was told yesterday of a cancer diagnosis says to the nurse, "I do not think I want chemotherapy. What is the point of any of this?" The client looks tired and is looking down at the bed sheet.
stem: Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Your doctor knows what is best, so you should follow the plan your doctor has recommended."
"It sounds like you feel discouraged. Can you tell me what worries you most?"
"Many people feel this way at first, but you need to stay positive and keep fighting."
"Why would you decide something like that so soon after hearing the diagnosis?"
rationale: 1) Identify the client's emotional state: discouraged, possibly overwhelmed after news from yesterday. 2) Recall that therapeutic communication reflects feelings and uses open-ended prompts. 3) Eliminate advice-giving (follow the plan). 4) Eliminate false reassurance and telling the client to stay positive. 5) Eliminate why-questions because they feel judgmental. 6) Choose the reflecting, open-ended response.
optionRationales: Gives advice and shuts down the client's concerns; it also ignores the client's right to decide.
Reflects the feeling and invites the client to explore it, which opens communication and helps the client's concerns surface before decisions are made.
Offers false reassurance and a directive that dismisses the client's feelings.
A why-question can feel judgmental and make the client defensive.
strategy: Communication: reflect and explore
keyFacts: Reflect the feeling and use open-ended prompts.
Avoid advice, false reassurance and why-questions.

vignette: A 60-year-old client is scheduled for surgery in two hours. The surgeon's office left a consent form on the chart. The nurse finds the client drowsy and slurring speech 30 minutes after a prescribed preoperative sedative. The client's adult child is at the bedside and offers to sign for the client. The client has no known impairment of decision making.
stem: Which action should the nurse take?
options: Have the client sign now and witness the signature to avoid delaying the scheduled surgery
Accept the adult child's signature since the client is drowsy and cannot read the form
Hold the form and notify the surgeon that consent must wait until the client is alert
Explain the surgical risks to the client and then obtain the signature before the surgery
rationale: 1) Identify the issue: consent in a client affected by sedation. 2) Recall the elements: capacity, adequate information, voluntary choice. 3) Sedation impairs capacity right now, so a signature is not valid. 4) The child cannot sign because the client is normally competent. 5) The nurse witnesses the signature but does not provide the informing; that duty belongs to the surgeon. 6) Choose to delay signing and notify the surgeon, advocating for the client.
optionRationales: The client's sedation undermines the validity of consent, so a signature now would not be informed or voluntary.
A relative signs only when the client lacks decision-making capacity; this client had capacity before sedation and should decide.
Consent is valid only if the client is competent, informed and not under the effect of sedation. The surgeon is responsible for the explanation and for obtaining consent.
Explaining the procedure and its risks is the surgeon's responsibility, and consent should not be sought from a sedated client.
strategy: Ethics: autonomy and advocacy
keyFacts: Informed consent requires capacity, information and voluntariness.
The provider performing the procedure is responsible for obtaining consent; the nurse witnesses and advocates.

vignette: A nurse prepares to give a prescribed intravenous potassium replacement to a 70-year-old client with a low potassium level who has been vomiting. The medication arrives from pharmacy, and the client has a peripheral intravenous line. The client's urine output over the last shift was very low.
stem: Which action is most important before giving the medication?
options: Report the very low urine output to the provider before giving the potassium
Give it as a slow intravenous push over several minutes with the cardiac monitor on
Ask the client when the last meal was and hold the dose if the client has eaten
Check the client's name band and proceed since pharmacy verified the order
rationale: 1) Identify the drug class: potassium is a high-alert medication. 2) Think about what makes it dangerous: concentration, rate and poor excretion. 3) Low urine output suggests kidneys may not excrete potassium well, so the provider must know. 4) Eliminate push administration, which raises cardiac risk. 5) Eliminate options about meals and identification alone because they do not match the risk. 6) Choose verifying dilution and rate on a pump and reporting the low urine output.
optionRationales: Poor kidney excretion raises the risk of dangerous potassium levels, so the very low urine output must be reported before giving the dose. Potassium is a high-alert medication and is infused diluted at a controlled rate, not pushed.
Rapid or push administration of potassium can cause dangerous cardiac effects; it is infused diluted at a controlled rate.
Food intake is irrelevant to intravenous potassium and does not address the safety risk.
Identification is necessary but not sufficient; proceeding without addressing the low urine output ignores the high-alert risk.
strategy: Safety: match monitoring to risk
keyFacts: Potassium is a high-alert medication given diluted at a controlled rate, not as an intravenous push.
Check urine output and renal status before giving potassium.

vignette: A nurse is preparing a 55-year-old client with diabetes for discharge home on day 3 after open abdominal surgery. The incision is closed with staples and the client lives with a spouse who will help. The client is eager to return to gardening and asks about everything except warning signs. The nurse has limited time before the transport arrives.
stem: Which instruction should the nurse give the highest priority?
options: Hold a pillow firmly over the incision when coughing or changing position
Take the prescribed pain medicine before walking so activity is comfortable
Walk short distances several times a day and increase the distance gradually
Call the surgeon the same day if the wound turns hot, swollen or leaks pus
rationale: 1) The stem asks for the highest priority, so rank by risk of harm. 2) Four teaching points are all correct for this client, so none can be eliminated as wrong, only ranked. 3) Splinting, timing of pain medicine and gradual walking improve comfort and recovery, and the client will likely do them anyway. 4) The client has diabetes and a stapled wound, which raises the risk of infection, and the client is not asking about warning signs, so this knowledge gap carries the greatest danger. 5) Choose teaching on when to call for help.
optionRationales: Splinting reduces strain on the wound and is good teaching, but a client who misses it has discomfort rather than an unrecognized emergency.
Pain control supports walking and recovery. It is useful teaching but the client is likely to seek relief and it does not protect against unrecognized complications.
Gradual walking supports circulation and recovery and is an important routine instruction. It is a healthy habit, not a response to a dangerous change.
Recognizing and reporting early signs of wound infection prevents serious complications. The client has diabetes and has not asked about warning signs, so this gap carries the highest risk.
strategy: Discharge: complication warning signs first
keyFacts: Discharge teaching should cover warning signs and when to call before comfort and lifestyle advice.
Diabetes slows healing and raises the risk of wound infection.

vignette: A nurse on a surgical unit begins the morning shift with four clients and a short time to see each of them. All are stable enough to be on the unit, and all have a documented fluid or electrolyte concern. The nurse must decide whom to assess first.
stem: Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with long-standing heart failure whose ankle swelling matches the admission note
A client with chronic kidney disease whose daily weight is steady and who has mild itching
A client after bowel surgery with falling urine output, rising pulse and new dizziness
A client on nasogastric suction who reports thirst and dry lips, with vital signs at baseline
rationale: 1) The stem asks who to see first, so sort by acute versus chronic and stable versus unstable. 2) Chronic problems with unchanged findings (heart failure swelling, kidney disease with steady weight) are lower priority. 3) Thirst and dry lips with baseline vital signs on suction are expected and manageable, but need follow-up. 4) A new fall in urine output with rising pulse and dizziness after surgery suggests developing volume loss or bleeding, an acute change in an early postoperative client. 5) Choose the acute, changing client.
optionRationales: Swelling that matches the admission note is chronic and unchanged, so it is a lower priority than a new change.
Steady weight and mild itching in chronic kidney disease are stable and long-standing, though they still need care later.
Falling urine output, rising pulse and orthostatic dizziness are new and point to volume loss or bleeding after surgery. This is the acute and potentially unstable client.
Thirst on suction is an expected consequence and vital signs are at baseline, so this client is stable and can be seen after the unstable client.
strategy: Acute before chronic
keyFacts: Acute and new findings take priority over chronic findings that are unchanged from baseline.
After surgery, falling urine output with rising pulse and dizziness can signal volume loss or bleeding and needs prompt assessment.

topic: Evaluation step of the nursing process
vignette: A nurse raised the head of the bed and gave oxygen as prescribed to a client with shortness of breath. The care plan goal was a respiratory rate in the normal range and effort that is easier. One hour later the nurse returns, counts the respirations, checks the saturation, and compares the results with the goal.
stem: Which step of the nursing process is the nurse performing?
options: Assessment
Evaluation
Planning
Implementation
rationale: 1) Underline the verb: compares the results with the goal. 2) Recall the five steps: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, evaluation. 3) Goal comparison after an intervention means evaluation. 4) Assessment also involves measuring, which is the trap. 5) Planning and implementation already occurred. 6) Choose evaluation.
optionRationales: Tempting because the nurse collects data, but the purpose here is to judge progress toward a goal, not to gather initial data.
The nurse is comparing the client's response with the stated goal, which defines evaluation.
Planning involves setting goals and choosing interventions, which were already completed.
The interventions (positioning, oxygen) were already carried out; this step is checking their result.
strategy: Nursing process: match the verb
keyFacts: Evaluation compares client response with expected outcomes.
Data collection can occur in assessment and in evaluation; the purpose differs.

vignette: A 28-year-old client arrives after a motorcycle collision with a suspected abdominal bleed. On arrival the client is awake and anxious, the systolic blood pressure is in the normal range, the pulse is 112 beats per minute and the skin is cool. Intravenous access is placed and fluids are started. The nurse reassesses thirty minutes later.
stem: Which reassessment finding most strongly suggests the client is no longer compensating?
options: Growing confusion with a blood pressure now trending downward
A heart rate that has risen slightly since the first reading
A new complaint of thirst along with a dry mouth and dry lips
Cool and pale skin that remains unchanged on the arms and legs
rationale: 1) The clue is the word no longer: the client has already shown compensation (tachycardia, cool skin) with a normal pressure. 2) The question asks what shows compensation failing, not what shows shock exists. 3) Thirst, a small rise in heart rate, and persistent cool skin are consistent with ongoing compensation and early volume loss. 4) Falling blood pressure with changing mental status means the brain and body are no longer perfused, which is decompensation and a late, dangerous sign. 5) Choose the finding that marks a change in trend.
optionRationales: Falling pressure with new confusion shows compensation is failing and perfusion of the brain is dropping. This is a late, dangerous trend that needs immediate escalation.
A small rise in heart rate fits a compensating body that is still maintaining pressure, so it does not show failure on its own.
Thirst is an early sign of fluid loss and is expected while the body compensates.
Cool skin was already present and fits vasoconstriction during compensation, so an unchanged finding does not show a new decline.
strategy: Trend: compensation failing
keyFacts: Falling blood pressure with changed mental status is a late sign that compensation has failed in shock.
Tachycardia, thirst, and cool skin are early signs while blood pressure is still maintained.

vignette: A nurse is caring for a 40-year-old client with a chest tube connected to a water-seal drainage system after trauma to the chest. The client needs to be taken to radiology for imaging. The nurse reviews safe management of the system.
stem: Which action by the nurse is inappropriate?
options: Keeping the drainage system below the level of the chest during transport
Checking that the tubing connections are secure and taped before leaving
Watching for fluctuation of water in the water-seal chamber with breathing
Clamping the chest tube during the trip to radiology without an order
rationale: 1) Notice the stem asks what is INAPPROPRIATE, so three options will be safe. 2) Test each: below chest level, secure connections and watching fluctuation all follow standard practice. 3) Clamping stops air and fluid escaping, which can cause pressure to build in the chest. 4) Select the option that breaks the rule.
optionRationales: Correct; this helps drainage and prevents fluid from flowing back into the chest.
Correct; air leaks or disconnections can compromise the system.
Correct; expected fluctuation shows the system communicates with the pleural space.
Clamping without an order can trap air and fluid and lead to a tension pneumothorax. The tube is normally left unclamped unless a provider orders otherwise.
strategy: Negative stem: find the odd one
keyFacts: Keep the chest drainage system below the chest and the tube unclamped unless ordered.
Fluctuation in the water-seal chamber is expected with breathing.

vignette: A 67-year-old client on day 3 after a hip replacement suddenly reports sharp chest pain and shortness of breath. The client is anxious and sweating, with a pulse of 122/min, respirations of 30/min and oxygen saturation of 88% on room air.
stem: Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Complete a full head-to-toe assessment before calling the provider
Raise the head of the bed and apply oxygen per protocol
Stay with the client and coach slow breathing with a calm voice
Ambulate the client to promote circulation and expand the lungs
rationale: 1) Recognize the pattern: sudden chest pain and dyspnea after surgery and immobility, with tachycardia and low saturation. 2) Classify the client as unstable, so the rule is to act and support, not complete a long assessment. 3) Apply ABC and Maslow: breathing and oxygenation first. 4) Eliminate full assessment (delay), emotional coaching (not the priority), and ambulation (increases oxygen demand). 5) Choose positioning and oxygen, then call for help.
optionRationales: Assessment is normally first, but this client is unstable; delay in support worsens hypoxemia.
The picture suggests a pulmonary embolism. Oxygenation is the first physiological need, and this client is unstable, so the nurse acts to support breathing, then calls for help.
Empathic and helpful, but anxiety is secondary here; it does not correct hypoxemia.
Activity could worsen the situation and increases oxygen demand; a suspected clot calls for rest.
strategy: Exception: unstable client needs action now
keyFacts: Sudden dyspnea and chest pain after surgery may indicate pulmonary embolism.
In an unstable client, support oxygenation first and summon help.

vignette: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who takes insulin is found on a medical unit sweating, trembling, and irritable shortly before lunch, about 90 minutes after his scheduled insulin dose. He is awake, answers questions slowly, and can hold a cup without help. A bedside glucose reading is below the normal range.
stem: Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Hold the next scheduled insulin dose and notify the provider about the low glucose reading
Give a fast-acting oral carbohydrate such as fruit juice and recheck the glucose afterward
Prepare to give a glucagon injection because he is slow to respond when the nurse speaks to him
Start an intravenous line and request an order for dextrose to correct the low glucose
rationale: 1) The signs (sweating, tremor, irritability, slow responses) plus a low reading confirm hypoglycemia, so the problem is already identified and the stem asks what to do first. 2) Low glucose is a physiological threat, so it is treated before paperwork or notification (Maslow). 3) Choose the safest least invasive route that works: he is awake and can hold a cup, so he can swallow safely. 4) Glucagon and IV dextrose are for clients who cannot take food by mouth, so they skip a step. 5) Notifying the provider and holding insulin are appropriate but come after treatment. 6) Recheck the glucose afterward to confirm the response.
optionRationales: Tempting because the provider should know and insulin may need adjusting, but this is the correct action in the wrong order: the low glucose must be treated before anything else.
Correct. He is awake and able to swallow, so an oral fast-acting carbohydrate is the quickest, safest, least invasive treatment; recheck the glucose afterward.
Glucagon is kept for clients who cannot safely swallow or who are unresponsive. He is slow but awake and holding a cup, so a less invasive option comes first.
An IV with dextrose is for clients who cannot take food by mouth and needs an order and time to set up; it is more invasive than needed for an alert client.
strategy: Maslow: treat the physiological threat first
keyFacts: Alert and able to swallow with low glucose: give a fast-acting oral carbohydrate, then recheck.
Glucagon or IV dextrose is for the client who cannot swallow or is unresponsive.

vignette: A 44-year-old woman is on the surgical unit on the evening after a total thyroidectomy. She has been awake and conversing since returning from the recovery area. Over the next hour she reports several concerns to the nurse, who is deciding which one needs attention first.
stem: Which client report or finding requires the nurse to act first?
options: Hoarse voice that has stayed the same since she woke up from anesthesia
Tingling and numbness around her mouth and in the tips of her fingers
Increasing neck swelling with a high-pitched sound heard on inspiration
Incisional soreness rated as moderate that eases when she changes position
rationale: 1) Name the surgery and its two classic dangers: airway compromise from bleeding or swelling in the neck, and low calcium if the parathyroid glands are injured or removed. 2) The stem asks which to act on first, so rank the problems. 3) Apply ABCs: airway outranks every other concern. 4) Increasing neck swelling with a high-pitched inspiratory sound suggests the airway is narrowing. 5) Tingling around the mouth suggests low calcium and must be reported promptly, but it is a metabolic problem that develops over hours and does not close the airway immediately. 6) Unchanged hoarseness and manageable soreness are common and expected early on.
optionRationales: Hoarseness can result from airway tube irritation or swelling and is common early; it is stable and does not show a worsening trend.
Tempting because it suggests low calcium, a real complication that needs prompt reporting. It is not the first priority because it does not threaten the airway at this moment.
Correct. Increasing swelling with a high-pitched sound on inspiration points to a narrowing airway, which is the most immediate life threat, so it is acted on first.
Moderate soreness that eases with repositioning is expected after surgery and responds to comfort measures; it is stable.
strategy: ABCs: airway before metabolic problems
keyFacts: After thyroidectomy, watch the airway (swelling, bleeding, stridor) and calcium (tingling, muscle spasm).
Airway compromise outranks metabolic complications when both are present.

vignette: A 63-year-old man with cirrhosis is admitted with increasing confusion and a flapping tremor when his arms are held out. The provider starts lactulose to lower the blood ammonia level. On the second day the nurse reviews his bowel pattern and mental status.
stem: Which finding best shows that the medication is having its intended effect?
options: Two to three soft stools daily along with improved orientation
No stool for a full day and confusion that is no better than before
Frequent watery stools with dizziness on standing from a seat
A single firm stool each day with the flapping tremor still present
rationale: 1) Identify the purpose: lactulose draws ammonia into the bowel and promotes stool so ammonia leaves the body; the goal is a modest number of soft stools. 2) The stem asks for the intended effect, so look for a finding that shows both a bowel response and a clinical improvement. 3) Eliminate findings that show too little effect (no stool, firm stool) because the ammonia is not being cleared. 4) Eliminate too much effect: watery stools with dizziness suggest fluid loss and a dose problem. 5) Confirm the correct option links the bowel pattern to better mental status.
optionRationales: Correct. A few soft stools show the drug is working, and better orientation shows the ammonia effect on the brain is easing.
No stool and unchanged confusion mean the drug has not produced the needed response, so ammonia is probably not being cleared.
Tempting because more stool seems like more ammonia removal, but watery stools with dizziness suggest volume depletion and a dose that is too strong.
A single firm stool is too little effect, and the persisting tremor shows no clinical improvement.
strategy: Expected effect vs too much of the drug
keyFacts: Lactulose goal in hepatic encephalopathy: a small number of soft stools per day, with improved mental status.
Excessive diarrhea is an adverse effect that can cause dehydration and electrolyte loss.

topic: Early signs of rising intracranial pressure
vignette: A 27-year-old man is admitted after a fall from a ladder with a head injury. For the first six hours his vital signs have been steady and his pupils equal and reactive. The nurse is checking him every hour and wants to detect any rise in intracranial pressure as early as possible.
stem: Which new finding is the earliest sign of increasing intracranial pressure?
options: A dilated pupil on the injured side that does not react to light
Slowing heart rate with a rising systolic blood pressure
Stiff extension of the arms and legs in response to pain
New restlessness and slower responses to questions than before
rationale: 1) The stem asks for the earliest sign, not the most dramatic one, so think of the order in which findings appear. 2) The brain's higher centers are most sensitive to pressure, so a change in level of consciousness (restlessness, confusion, drowsiness, slower answers) appears first. 3) Pupil changes appear later as pressure affects the nerves to the eye. 4) Slowing heart rate with rising systolic pressure and abnormal posturing are late signs of severe pressure and impending herniation. 5) Choose the subtle early change; the dramatic options are tempting traps.
optionRationales: A fixed dilated pupil is a late sign of pressure on the brainstem nerves, not the earliest.
Bradycardia with rising systolic blood pressure is part of the late Cushing response.
Extension posturing signals severe brain dysfunction and is a late finding.
Correct. A decrease in level of consciousness, including restlessness and slower responses, is the earliest and most sensitive indicator of rising pressure.
strategy: Earliest sign = level of consciousness change
keyFacts: Change in level of consciousness is the earliest and most sensitive sign of increased intracranial pressure.
Bradycardia, rising systolic pressure, fixed pupils, and posturing are late signs.

topic: Seizure first aid and client safety
vignette: A 35-year-old woman with epilepsy is sitting in a chair in the day room of a rehabilitation unit when she stiffens, cries out, and begins rhythmic jerking of all four limbs. Two other clients are nearby and one calls for help. The nurse arrives within seconds.
stem: What is the nurse's initial action?
options: Hold her arms and legs firmly to limit the jerking
Place a padded object between her teeth to protect her tongue
Lower her to the floor and protect her head from injury
Apply supplemental oxygen and prepare a suction setup
rationale: 1) A seizure is under way and the immediate danger is injury from falling or striking objects. 2) Safety comes first when the client cannot protect herself. 3) The best first step is to lower her to a safe surface and cushion her head. 4) Never restrain the limbs, because this can cause fractures or muscle injury. 5) Never place anything in the mouth during a seizure, because it can break teeth or obstruct the airway. 6) Oxygen and suction may be needed afterward, but they are not the first step while the body is jerking. Note the time and turn her to the side when the jerking stops.
optionRationales: Restraining the limbs does not stop the seizure and can cause injury to her and to the nurse.
Objects in the mouth can break teeth or block the airway; this old practice is not safe.
Correct. Easing her to the floor and protecting her head prevents injury, which is the immediate danger while she cannot control her movements.
Tempting because airway matters, but equipment is not the first step when injury risk is immediate; it is used afterward as needed.
strategy: Safety first: prevent injury during the seizure
keyFacts: During a seizure: protect the head, loosen tight clothing, note the time, and do not restrain or put anything in the mouth.
After the seizure, turn the client to the side to keep the airway clear.

topic: Delegating tube feeding and glucose-related tasks
vignette: A registered nurse on a medical unit is assigning tasks to a nursing assistant whose competencies are current and whose duties are limited to what the facility allows. Four clients need care this morning. One client has a feeding tube placed an hour ago that has not yet been used. A second client was started on insulin yesterday and is new to injections. A third client with diabetes is drowsy and had a low fingerstick glucose reading ten minutes ago. A fourth client has received the same continuous tube feeding for two weeks and has been steady throughout. The nurse is also short of time and wants to hand off as many tasks as safely possible.
stem: Which task is the most appropriate for the nurse to delegate to the nursing assistant?
options: Verify the position of the feeding tube placed an hour ago before formula is started
Show the client newly started on insulin how to rotate injection sites at home
Decide whether the drowsy client's low glucose reading needs juice or a call to the provider
Record formula volume and urine output for the client on a long-standing tube feeding
rationale: 1) Delegation is decided by scope and client stability: the nurse keeps assessment, teaching, evaluation and clinical judgment, and the assistant takes routine, predictable tasks. 2) Confirming placement of a new feeding tube is an assessment with a risk of aspiration if wrong, so it stays with the nurse. 3) Teaching a new insulin user is a nursing responsibility. 4) Deciding how to respond to a low glucose in a drowsy client is interpretation and judgment about an unstable client. 5) Recording intake and output for a client who has been steady on the same feeding is routine and within the assistant's scope, with a request to report any change. 6) The key is the one task that needs no nursing judgment.
optionRationales: Right action, wrong person: checking tube placement before first use is a nursing assessment and cannot be handed off.
Right action for the nurse, but teaching and checking understanding are not delegated.
Plausible because glucose care is routine on this unit, but interpreting the result in a drowsy client and choosing treatment requires nursing judgment about an unstable client.
Correct. Recording volumes and urine output for a steady client is a routine task within the assistant's scope; the nurse reviews the totals and asks to be told of any change.
strategy: Delegation: routine tasks on stable clients; nurse keeps assess, teach, judge
keyFacts: Do not delegate assessment, teaching, evaluation, or decisions about unstable clients.
Routine intake and output recording on a steady tube-fed client may be delegated to a competent assistant.

vignette: A 72-year-old woman is preparing to go home after same-day cataract extraction on her right eye. The nurse reviews eye protection, activity, and warning signs. The client then restates her plan in her own words.
stem: Which statement by the client indicates that further teaching is needed?
options: I will wear the protective shield when I sleep at night
I will bend down to pick up my dog's food bowl each morning
I will call right away if I notice a sudden increase in eye pain
I will wash my hands before I put in the eye drops as prescribed
rationale: 1) The wording 'further teaching is needed' means three statements are correct and one is unsafe, so find the unsafe one. 2) Recall the goals after cataract surgery: protect the eye and avoid raising pressure in it. 3) Bending, straining, and lifting increase eye pressure and risk strain on the healing site. 4) The shield at night, hand washing before drops, and reporting sudden pain are all protective behaviors. 5) The statement about bending to the floor each morning shows a misunderstanding.
optionRationales: Correct teaching: a shield protects the eye from accidental rubbing or pressure while asleep.
Correct choice for further teaching. Bending low and heavy lifting increase eye pressure and can harm the healing site.
Appropriate: sudden pain or a drop in vision can signal a complication and must be reported promptly.
Appropriate: clean hands help prevent infection when putting in eye drops.
strategy: Negative stem: choose the unsafe statement
keyFacts: After cataract surgery avoid bending low, straining, heavy lifting, and rubbing the eye.
Report sudden pain, vision loss, or increasing redness or discharge.

topic: Rapid-acting insulin and a delayed meal
vignette: A nurse is about to give a scheduled mealtime dose of rapid-acting insulin to a 66-year-old woman on a medical unit. The order says to give it with the meal. The nurse learns the lunch trays will be about an hour late because of a kitchen equipment problem. The client is alert and her glucose is within her usual range.
stem: What is the most appropriate action by the nurse?
options: Hold the dose until the meal is at the bedside and ask dietary to speed up delivery
Give the dose on time as ordered and offer juice later when the tray finally arrives
Give a reduced amount of the dose now and the remainder when she begins her meal
Skip the dose, write in the record that the meal was late, and give the next one on time
rationale: 1) Insulin is a high-alert medication; the main danger is hypoglycemia when insulin acts without food. 2) Rapid-acting insulin starts working quickly, so it must be given when the meal is ready to be eaten. 3) Ask what the nurse can safely do within scope: adjust timing to the actual meal and solve the barrier. 4) Giving insulin now leaves about an hour of insulin action without food. 5) Changing the dose is outside the nurse's scope without a prescriber order. 6) Skipping a dose without a decision from the prescriber is a medication omission and risks high glucose. 7) Holding until the meal is at the bedside and speeding up delivery meets the order and protects the client.
optionRationales: Correct. The order is to give the insulin with the meal, so the nurse times it to the actual meal and works to resolve the delay.
Tempting because it follows the clock, but insulin would act for an hour with no food, which risks hypoglycemia; juice later does not make this safe.
The nurse cannot change an ordered dose on her own, and splitting the dose is not part of the order.
Omitting the dose is not necessary because the meal is coming, and an omission needs a provider decision; it could also cause high glucose.
strategy: High-alert drug: match timing to the meal
keyFacts: Rapid-acting insulin is given when the meal is about to be eaten, because it acts quickly.
Nurses time and verify high-alert drugs but do not alter ordered doses without a prescriber.

vignette: At the start of the shift a nurse on a medical-surgical unit receives report on four clients. (1) A 62-year-old man two days after bowel surgery who rates his incision pain 8 out of 10 and has asked twice for medication; his vital signs are within his usual range. (2) A 56-year-old man with cirrhosis who passed a black, sticky stool during the night; sitting up, his heart rate is 112 and his blood pressure is 96/58, and he says he is waiting for his breakfast tray. (3) A 34-year-old woman with Crohn disease who has had four loose stools overnight and a temperature of 37.9 C; she is drinking fluids and walking in the hall. (4) A 48-year-old man with type 2 diabetes whose fingerstick glucose is 66 before breakfast; he is alert and the breakfast tray is at his bedside.
stem: Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: The man two days after bowel surgery who rates his incision pain 8 out of 10
The man with cirrhosis who passed a black, sticky stool during the night
The woman with Crohn disease who has had loose stools and a mild temperature
The man with type 2 diabetes whose glucose is 66 before breakfast
rationale: 1) Sort the clients by threat to life and how fast it can worsen. 2) A black, sticky stool in a client with cirrhosis suggests upper gastrointestinal bleeding, and a heart rate of 112 with a blood pressure of 96/58 shows his circulation is already compromised, so he is unstable. 3) The postoperative client's pain is real and needs attention, but his vital signs are stable, so it can follow. 4) The Crohn client has mild fever and loose stools but is drinking and walking. 5) A glucose of 66 in an alert client who can eat is fixed in minutes with the tray at the bedside. 6) Choose the client whose circulation is threatened.
optionRationales: Tempting because pain is the loudest complaint, but his vital signs are steady; medicating him matters, yet it is not a threat to life.
Correct. Black stool with a fast pulse and a low-normal blood pressure suggests bleeding with falling volume; circulation takes priority and he needs help now.
Symptomatic and worth follow-up, but she is hydrating and walking, and a mild temperature with loose stools is an expected pattern in her condition.
A glucose of 66 needs prompt attention, but this client is alert and can take food at the bedside, so it can be treated quickly after the unstable client is seen.
strategy: Circulation threat before pain, mild fever, or treatable glucose
keyFacts: Black, sticky stool suggests upper GI bleeding; a rising heart rate with a falling blood pressure signals volume loss.
Rank clients by threat to life: unstable circulation before pain, mild fever, or an easily treated glucose.

vignette: A 49-year-old man is newly diagnosed with gastroesophageal reflux disease after months of burning in the chest after meals and at night. The nurse is giving him instructions on lifestyle changes that reduce symptoms.
stem: Which instruction by the nurse is NOT appropriate for this client?
options: Lie down for a rest right after eating the evening meal
Raise the head of the bed using blocks under the frame
Eat smaller meals and avoid eating close to bedtime
Limit high-fat foods and avoid foods that trigger symptoms
rationale: 1) The word NOT means three instructions are appropriate and one is harmful. 2) Reflux happens when stomach contents move up into the esophagus, so anything that increases pressure or lets gravity push contents upward makes symptoms worse. 3) Lying flat soon after eating makes reflux more likely. 4) Raising the head of the bed, eating smaller meals, avoiding late meals, and limiting fat and trigger foods all reduce reflux. 5) Select the instruction that goes against these principles.
optionRationales: Correct choice for NOT appropriate. Lying down right after a meal lets stomach contents move upward and worsens reflux.
Appropriate: elevating the head of the bed uses gravity to keep stomach contents down at night.
Appropriate: smaller meals reduce stomach pressure, and avoiding late meals lets the stomach empty before lying down.
Appropriate: high-fat foods and known triggers can worsen reflux, so limiting them helps.
strategy: NOT stem: find the instruction that worsens reflux
keyFacts: Reflux self-care: stay upright after meals, elevate the head of the bed, eat smaller meals, and avoid late meals.
Common triggers include high-fat foods, caffeine, alcohol, and smoking.

vignette: A 40-year-old woman with Addison disease has been vomiting for two days and could not keep down her daily steroid replacement. In the emergency department she is weak and lightheaded and has a low blood pressure. The nurse anticipates laboratory results that reflect too little adrenal hormone.
stem: Which pattern of laboratory results does the nurse most expect?
options: High sodium, low potassium, high glucose
Low sodium, low potassium, high glucose
Low sodium, high potassium, low glucose
High sodium, high potassium, low glucose
rationale: 1) Name the problem: adrenal crisis from too little cortisol and aldosterone, triggered by missing her replacement. 2) Aldosterone normally holds sodium and water and removes potassium, so a shortage causes low sodium (and low volume and pressure) with high potassium. 3) Cortisol helps raise glucose, so a shortage tends to cause low glucose. 4) Match the pattern: low sodium, high potassium, low glucose. 5) The other options each break at least one link; the opposite pattern would suggest too much of these hormones.
optionRationales: This is closer to the opposite picture, with excess hormone effects that retain sodium, lose potassium, and raise glucose.
Low sodium fits, but low potassium and high glucose do not; a lack of aldosterone causes potassium to rise and a lack of cortisol lowers glucose.
Correct. Too little aldosterone lowers sodium and raises potassium, and too little cortisol lowers glucose.
High sodium does not fit because a lack of aldosterone causes sodium loss.
strategy: Link the hormone deficit to the lab pattern
keyFacts: Adrenal insufficiency: low sodium, high potassium, low glucose, low blood pressure.
Missed steroid doses or illness can trigger adrenal crisis, which is an emergency.

vignette: A 15-year-old girl with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes is preparing for discharge. She tells the nurse she will not take her insulin at school and says, 'Everyone will stare at me and I just want to be normal.' Her glucose has been stable in the hospital and she has demonstrated the injection technique correctly.
stem: Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
options: You have to take it at school, or you will end up back in the hospital
Most teenagers manage this well at school, so I am sure you will be fine too
I will speak to your classmates so that nobody stares at you while you inject
It sounds like you are worried about being seen as different. Tell me more.
rationale: 1) The client voices a feeling (fear of being different), not a knowledge gap, because she can already inject correctly. 2) Therapeutic communication responds to the feeling first. 3) Threats and warnings add pressure and may close the conversation. 4) False reassurance dismisses her concern. 5) Solving the problem for her without asking removes her control and may embarrass her. 6) Reflecting the feeling and inviting her to say more builds trust and opens the way to joint problem solving.
optionRationales: This is a threat that uses fear; it ignores her feeling and is likely to make her defensive.
False reassurance dismisses her concern and tells her how she will feel.
Tempting because it tries to help, but it takes over without asking what she wants and could increase her embarrassment.
Correct. It reflects her feeling and invites her to explain, which supports the relationship and leads to shared problem solving.
strategy: Reflect feelings; open-ended, not reassurance
keyFacts: Respond to feelings before facts; use reflection and open-ended invitations.
Adolescents value peer acceptance; involve them in planning how to manage diabetes at school.

vignette: A 74-year-old man was admitted two hours ago with sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech. While lying flat he becomes drowsy, saliva is pooling in his mouth, and his breathing has a gurgling sound. His oxygen saturation is lower than it was on admission. The nurse is at the bedside.
stem: What is the priority nursing action?
options: Complete a full neurologic assessment, including the Glasgow Coma Scale, before other care
Position him on his side with the head slightly raised and suction the mouth gently
Perform a bedside swallowing screen before giving him anything to eat or drink by mouth
Notify the provider about the change in his condition and wait for new orders
rationale: 1) Gurgling breathing, pooled saliva, drowsiness, and a falling saturation show a partly blocked airway and early failure of airway protection. 2) The airway is the first of the ABCs and it outranks assessment, screening, and notification. 3) Here the problem is already found, so assessing further would delay treatment: act now. 4) The simplest effective action is to position him to let secretions drain and remove them with suction. 5) A swallowing screen is not appropriate in a drowsy client who cannot protect the airway. 6) The provider should be informed right after the airway is secured, with the findings ready to report.
optionRationales: Tempting because assessing is usually first, but the airway problem is already evident and a long assessment delays clearing secretions.
Correct. Positioning on the side with the head slightly raised and suctioning clears the secretions and protects the airway, the top priority.
A swallowing screen requires an alert client who can cooperate; this client is drowsy and cannot protect the airway.
Notification is needed, but it follows the airway action; waiting for orders delays care for a threatened airway.
strategy: ABCs: clear the airway before assessing or calling
keyFacts: Airway, breathing, circulation come before neurologic assessment, screening, and notification.
Stroke clients are at risk for aspiration; keep suction available and make nothing by mouth until swallowing is screened.

vignette: A 38-year-old man was admitted two days after a viral illness with weakness that is moving upward from his legs, and he has been diagnosed with Guillain-Barre syndrome. During the shift the nurse reviews his trend. The weakness has reached the hips, the ankle reflexes are absent, he has had no bowel movement since admission, and he now stops to take a breath in the middle of a sentence.
stem: Which finding represents the greatest threat and requires immediate follow-up?
options: Needing to pause for breath in the middle of a spoken sentence
Absent ankle reflexes on both sides noted on the neurologic exam
Weakness that has spread upward from the legs to the hips
Not having had a bowel movement since being admitted to the unit
rationale: 1) Decide which findings are expected for the disease and which signal instability. 2) In Guillain-Barre syndrome, ascending weakness and absent reflexes are expected features. 3) Constipation is common with immobility and nerve involvement but is not urgent. 4) The danger is that weakness reaches the muscles of breathing. 5) Breathlessness during speech suggests falling respiratory function: breathing outranks all other findings (ABCs). 6) The nurse should act at once, check respiratory function, and call for help as policy requires.
optionRationales: Correct. Pausing to breathe mid-sentence suggests the respiratory muscles are weakening, which can progress to respiratory failure, so it needs immediate action.
Absent reflexes are an expected feature of the disease and are not an urgent change.
Weakness spreading upward is expected and should be monitored, but it is a trend; it becomes critical when breathing is affected.
No bowel movement is a common problem that can be managed after the airway and breathing are protected.
strategy: Expected findings vs a life threat: breathing first
keyFacts: Guillain-Barre syndrome causes ascending weakness; monitor breathing closely because the respiratory muscles can fail.
Absent reflexes are expected; breathing difficulty is the urgent finding.

vignette: A 29-year-old man had a short leg cast applied six hours ago after a tibial fracture. He tells the nurse his pain has climbed steadily and now feels deep and burning, even though an opioid analgesic was given 45 minutes ago. The leg is resting elevated on a pillow and the toes look slightly swollen. He winces when the nurse gently moves his toes and says they feel tight and tingly. His roommate suggests the cast simply needs time to settle.
stem: Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask the provider for an earlier analgesic dose because the pain is poorly controlled
Telephone the provider to report the pain and ask for an order to bivalve the cast
Compare toe color, warmth, sensation, movement, and pulses with the other foot
Cut along the cast with the cast cutter to relieve pressure over the swollen area
rationale: 1) Pain that is increasing and out of proportion despite an analgesic, with tightness, tingling and pain on toe movement, may mean compartment syndrome, a limb-threatening emergency. 2) The data are incomplete, so the first action is to assess: a neurovascular check of color, warmth, sensation, movement and pulses, compared with the other foot. 3) The assessment is followed by an urgent report to the provider with those findings, not a delay. 4) More analgesic treats a symptom and can mask the warning sign. 5) Calling before assessing is the right action at the wrong time, since the report needs the findings. 6) Opening or cutting a cast is outside the nurse's scope without an order and skill, and could harm the client.
optionRationales: Fits a client with ordinary fracture pain, but here extra analgesic can hide a developing circulation problem and delays finding the cause.
Right action, wrong time: the provider must be told promptly, but the report should carry assessment findings, so the nurse checks the limb first and then calls urgently.
Correct. A neurovascular check compared with the other foot supplies the findings needed for an urgent report to the provider, who decides about relieving pressure.
Plausible because pressure is the problem, but cutting a cast is outside the nurse's scope without an order and training, and it is not the first step.
strategy: Nursing process: assess first, then report urgently
keyFacts: Pain out of proportion that is unrelieved by analgesics, with tightness and tingling, may signal compartment syndrome.
Neurovascular check: color, warmth, sensation, movement, pulses, compared with the other limb, then report urgently.

vignette: A 5-week-old boy is brought to the clinic because he has had forceful vomiting after most feedings for three days. The vomit is milk without bile and he seems hungry again right afterward. His weight is lower than at the last visit, he has had two wet diapers in the past day, and his anterior fontanelle looks slightly sunken. The nurse can feel a small olive-shaped mass in the upper abdomen. His parents have slept little, say they feel they are failing him, and have been propping him upright after feedings as they read online.
stem: Which concern should the nurse address first?
options: The parents are exhausted and fear that feeding trouble is harming their bond
The baby has lost weight and is not receiving enough calories for growth
The parents have not been shown the best way to position him after feeding
The baby is losing more fluid by vomiting than he is able to take in
rationale: 1) The picture suggests an obstruction at the stomach outlet with repeated forceful vomiting. 2) Infants have little fluid reserve, and few wet diapers with a sunken fontanelle show that fluid loss is already affecting him. 3) Fluid and electrolyte balance is a physiological need that must be corrected before anything else. 4) Weight loss and low calorie intake are true, but they develop over days and cannot be addressed until he is rehydrated. 5) Positioning advice would suit a baby with simple reflux, and the parents' distress is real, but both rank below a physiological threat. 6) Choose the concern that threatens him now.
optionRationales: Real and worth supporting, but it is a psychosocial need and ranks below a physiological threat.
True and important, but nutritional deficit builds over time; the fluid loss is the more immediate danger in a small infant.
Right action for an infant with simple reflux, but positioning does not fix an obstruction and teaching ranks below the physiological problem.
Correct. Fewer wet diapers and a sunken fontanelle show dehydration is under way in an infant who compensates poorly, so fluid balance comes first.
strategy: Maslow: fluid balance before nutrition, teaching, and bonding
keyFacts: Infants dehydrate quickly; signs include a sunken fontanelle and fewer wet diapers.
Forceful non-bilious vomiting with an olive-shaped mass suggests pyloric stenosis.

vignette: A 52-year-old woman is starting levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. She also takes a calcium supplement for bone health. The nurse teaches her about the medication and then asks her to describe in her own words how she will take it.
stem: Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?
options: I will stop taking the pill once my energy has returned to normal and I feel well again
I will take it each morning at the same time on an empty stomach, apart from calcium
I will take an extra pill on days when I feel very tired to give me more energy
I will take it with my breakfast and my calcium supplement so that I remember both
rationale: 1) The stem tests whether the client's own words show safe self-management of thyroid hormone replacement. 2) Replacement therapy is usually lifelong and taken consistently; feeling better is a sign that it is working, not a reason to stop. 3) Extra doses can cause too much thyroid hormone with palpitations and anxiety. 4) Food and calcium can reduce absorption, so the drug is taken on an empty stomach and separated from calcium. 5) The correct statement shows regular timing, empty stomach, and separation from the supplement.
optionRationales: Energy returning shows the drug is working; stopping can bring the symptoms back, because replacement is generally ongoing.
Correct. Consistent timing, an empty stomach, and separation from calcium support steady absorption and safe use.
Taking extra doses to treat tiredness can cause an excess of thyroid hormone, with a racing heart and anxiety.
Tempting for convenience, but food and calcium can reduce absorption of the drug.
strategy: Evaluate learning: look for safe, consistent self-management
keyFacts: Levothyroxine: take consistently, usually in the morning on an empty stomach, and separate from calcium and iron.
Replacement is generally long-term; report palpitations, chest pain, or marked nervousness.

vignette: A 61-year-old man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has progressive swallowing difficulty and weight loss. He is alert, understands his illness and the choices, and tells the nurse he does not want a feeding tube. His daughter insists he must have it, saying 'He has to eat.' A tube placement is scheduled for the morning.
stem: What is the nurse's best action?
options: Reassure the daughter that the tube will be placed as scheduled despite his refusal
Explain to the client that without a feeding tube he will slowly starve to death
Explore his reasons, confirm he understands his options, and inform the provider
Ask the daughter to help persuade him to accept the tube before the procedure
rationale: 1) The client is alert and understands, so he has decision-making capacity, and a competent adult has the right to refuse treatment. 2) The nurse's role is to advocate and ensure the decision is informed, not to decide for him. 3) The daughter's wishes matter and can be heard, but she cannot consent or refuse for a capable client. 4) Frightening or pressuring the client violates his autonomy. 5) The best action explores his reasons, checks understanding, and informs the provider so the plan can be reviewed before the procedure. 6) The nurse documents the discussion.
optionRationales: Proceeding because of the daughter's insistence overrides the client's own right to decide.
A blunt, frightening statement is coercive and does not support an informed choice.
Correct. This respects autonomy, ensures the refusal is informed, and brings the provider in to review the plan before the procedure.
Enlisting the daughter to persuade him is pressure, which undermines voluntary decision making.
strategy: Autonomy: competent client decides; nurse advocates
keyFacts: A competent adult may refuse treatment after being informed; the family cannot override the decision.
The nurse advocates, confirms understanding, informs the provider, and documents.

topic: Naming the nursing process step after foot teaching
vignette: A nurse taught a 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and reduced feeling in his feet to inspect his feet daily. The care plan states the outcome: 'Client will describe and demonstrate daily foot inspection by the end of the week.' At the end of the week the nurse asks him to show how he checks his feet. He looks at the tops of his feet but skips the soles and the spaces between his toes, and he cannot say what he would report. The nurse concludes that the outcome was only partly met and notes that more teaching will be needed.
stem: Which phase of the nursing process does the nurse's conclusion represent?
options: Evaluation of care provided
Assessment of a new problem
Planning of revised teaching
Implementation of the plan
rationale: 1) Name the phase by what the nurse is doing at this moment, not by the topic. 2) The nurse has the written outcome from the plan and the client's performance, and decides the outcome was only partly met. 3) Judging results against a stated outcome is the evaluation phase. 4) Assessment is gathering data to find a problem, and the problem was already known. 5) Planning is writing new goals and actions, which will come next but has not happened yet. 6) Implementation was the teaching already given.
optionRationales: Correct. Comparing the client's performance with the written outcome and judging it partly met is evaluation.
The nurse is not searching for a new problem; the foot-care knowledge need was already identified.
Revising the teaching plan is likely the next step, but at this moment the nurse is judging results, not writing new actions.
Implementation was the teaching already delivered; observing the result of that teaching is not carrying out the plan.
strategy: Nursing process: judging results against a written outcome
keyFacts: Evaluation compares the client's response with the written outcome and judges whether it was met.
Return demonstration is a common way to evaluate learning.

vignette: A 70-year-old woman has watery diarrhea several times a day after a course of antibiotics, and stool testing confirms Clostridioides difficile infection. She has been placed in a private room. The nurse is reviewing precautions with a nursing assistant before they enter the room together.
stem: Which instruction is most important for the nurse to give?
options: Use alcohol-based hand rub before entering and after leaving the room
Wear a surgical mask whenever you enter the room to care for or talk with her
Wear gloves when you touch stool and skip the gown for routine bedside care
Wash hands with soap and water, and wear a gown and gloves for direct care
rationale: 1) Identify the organism and route: C. difficile spreads by contact with contaminated surfaces, hands, and stool, and it forms spores. 2) Choose contact precautions: gown and gloves for care, a private room, and dedicated equipment. 3) Spores are not reliably removed by alcohol-based hand rub, so washing hands with soap and water is required. 4) A surgical mask protects against droplets, which is the wrong route. 5) Gloves without a gown leave clothing exposed to contaminated surfaces. 6) The only option that fits the route is soap-and-water hand washing plus gown and gloves.
optionRationales: Tempting because alcohol rub is routine in most care, but it does not reliably remove C. difficile spores, so it is not enough here.
A surgical mask addresses droplet spread, which is not how this infection is transmitted.
Partial precautions leave the uniform exposed to contamination; a gown is part of contact precautions for care.
Correct. Contact precautions with a gown and gloves, plus washing with soap and water, address the route and the spores.
strategy: Infection control: match precautions to the route
keyFacts: C. difficile: contact precautions, gown and gloves, private room, and soap-and-water hand washing.
Alcohol-based rubs do not reliably kill the spores.

vignette: A nurse on an adult psychiatric unit is talking with a 34-year-old client admitted two days ago with major depression. In a flat, quiet voice the client says, 'I keep thinking everyone would be better off without me.' The client has been calm and cooperative all morning and is sitting alone in the day room.
stem: Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Stay with the client and ask directly whether there is a plan and intent to end their life
Ask the client to sign a written no-harm agreement and then return to the day room until later
Document the statement carefully and report it to the provider during end-of-shift handoff
Reassure the client that these feelings usually pass and invite them to join the afternoon group
